editorial.headline: Film Exhibition: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Film and audiovisual screenings are nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor considering Bali, the central fact about KBLI 59140 is stark: it cannot be registered there through PMA today. This activity covers the exhibition of films and other audiovisual works for audiences in cinemas, outdoor settings, and other screening venues. It also includes film screenings presented as part of film festivals, whether those festivals are managed by government or private organisers. The defining subject is public screening: the moment when a film or audiovisual work is brought before viewers, whether as a regular venue programme or a festival event.

Nationally, the record places the activity in the open category for foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100% under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. It is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar business scales. That national position is meaningful: the activity is not subject to a national foreign-ownership cap below full ownership. The scope is also broad enough to encompass different presentation settings, from cinemas to open-air screenings and festival programmes, while remaining anchored in the activity of showing films or audiovisual works to an audience.

Bali presents a different and decisive picture for PMA registration. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is recorded as Low or Medium-Low for every scope of this activity. That risk position places it within Bali’s province-wide rule blocking all Low and Medium-Low risk activities from PMA registration. The record identifies this as a permanent, island-wide moratorium, referenced to May 2026. The Bali status is therefore not a reduced foreign-ownership allowance or a conditional local ceiling: it is a block on the PMA registration route.

The distinction is important because both statements remain true at once. Nationally, foreign ownership may reach 100%. In Bali, however, the activity is blocked for PMA registration under the province’s risk-based moratorium. For founders, the national openness describes the activity’s general investment position; the Bali classification determines the current local outcome. A full national foreign-ownership ceiling does not create a Bali PMA registration path where the provincial moratorium blocks it.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is real, but it does not translate into a PMA registration route in Bali.
